one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens with the observation that the judiciary is often likened to the Church and the military -- all three are bastions of conservatism bound by historical respect for traditions, precedents, meritocracy, and seniority. That makes the recent speech of Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo 'pleasantly surprising' yet deserving of acclaim: Gesmundo accepted the challenge of how the judiciary can 'turn tech for good and move from problem to solution' and acknowledged that 'AI has the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of judicial decisions, while at the same time, raise some algorithmic bias.' Panganiban catalogues the new lingo that magistrates need to learn -- algorithmic, tech, AI, Gen AI, ChatGPT (Generative Pretrained Transformer), Bard, Bing, Baidu, neuralink, bitcoin, crypto, metaverse, pod, 5G -- and points to the Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovation 2022-2027 (SPJI) unveiled by the SC a year earlier (deferring detailed exposition to his Nov 14 and 21, 2022 columns). His standard for judging SPJI is generous: even if just one SPJI objective is attained -- speeding up the delivery of quality justice by faithfully observing the Constitution's time limits for final decisions and hastening interlocutory orders -- the Court 'would have achieved a monumental success,' and a 2028-2033 extension with greater hi-tech and AI reliance could compound the gains. He sketches a civilizational-acceleration narrative -- agriculture and industrial revolution took centuries, jets/shinkansen/expressways took decades, then PC 1980s, internet 1990s, smartphone 2000s, cloud computing 2010s, AI 2020s -- and predicts that AI will transform jobs, professions, workplaces, habits, lifestyles, medicine, family relations, longevity, laws, and governance, inducing anxiety and fear of obsolescence; physical ailments may be healed by better medicine but mental disorders 'will become more prevalent and harder to cure.' Yet for every job outmoded, new ones will emerge -- just as tractors and backhoes replaced horses and carabao -- and enduring human values like 'empathy, trust, love, justice, and faith in the Almighty will remain.' His boundary thesis: 'humane justice can be dispensed only by judges, not always by an automated formula' -- because the Penal Code grants a range of penalties to select from and the Civil Code grants the liberality to make 'right and justice' prevail, conferring wide discretion not available to tech bots, to attain a just and humane society where liberty is safeguarded and prosperity is nurtured under the rule of law. On a personal note, he credits his continuing relevance in the hypersonic age to three disciplines: chair roles in international groups (Asean Law Association, Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague) and officer/director/trustee/adviser roles in leading banks, corporations, foundations, and charitable/religious organizations; faithful weekly column-writing for almost 17 years 'without fail despite occasional illness, travel, holidays, disability, death of loved ones'; and access to golf and tennis clubs where he plays several times weekly for physical, mental, and social well-being.
